messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Ellison is a 53-year-old married social worker of mixed North American heritage who presented for an initial psychological assessment following a sexual assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. He had spent nearly a year attempting to manage what was happening to him on his own before his wife's quiet, persistent concern and a gradual deterioration in his ability to function at work finally persuaded him to seek help.

The assault took place in a stairwell of a municipal building where Marcus had been attending an evening inter-agency meeting. He had stepped away from the conference room to take a phone call, descended one flight to find a quieter spot, and was cornered in the landing between floors by a man he did not recognize. The stairwell was narrow and windowless, the door above him had swung shut, and the sound of the meeting above was entirely inaudible. The assault lasted several minutes. When it was over the man left and Marcus stood alone in that enclosed concrete space, unable at first to move or speak, the fluorescent light above him flickering. He eventually returned to the meeting and said nothing. He drove home and said nothing. He told himself, in the weeks that followed, that he was processing it in the way he knew how — he was, after all, a professional who had spent decades helping others through trauma.

He was not processing it. What was happening instead was a slow reorganization of his daily life around the event's aftermath. He stopped using stairwells entirely, then began avoiding any room he could not immediately exit — small offices, examination rooms, elevator cars. In his work as a social worker, this became impossible to conceal indefinitely. His caseload involves home visits and meetings in community health centers, and he began declining referrals that required him to meet clients in unfamiliar buildings, telling his supervisor he was managing capacity. He has not visited a new location for a client in nearly eight months. Colleagues have noticed. His supervisor raised it formally last month, and Marcus could not offer an explanation that satisfied either of them.

When memory of the assault surfaces — and it surfaces often — what Marcus reports is not a narrative he can recount so much as a return to the landing. He has described sitting in a supervision session and suddenly feeling the cold of the stairwell wall against his back, the terror arriving whole, unchanged, as if no time has passed at all. What accompanies it and perhaps disturbs him more than the terror itself is the shame — a shame he struggles to articulate even now, knowing intellectually what he knows as a clinician about sexual violence and about men as survivors. He has said in session that he knows what happened, he can see it clearly enough, but when he tries to put it into language something stops working. The words simply do not come in any form that feels adequate or true.

Much of his private mental life is occupied by thoughts of the man in the stairwell — specifically, by detailed, recurring mental rehearsals of confrontation and retribution. He has come to believe that finding the man and making him account for what he did is the only resolution that would mean anything. He has also tried, with considerable effort, to simply not think about any of it, to push the images and the shame and the revenge scenarios out of his mind entirely, though he acknowledges this has had limited success.

Outside the house he moves through the world with a vigilance that exhausts him. He checks behind himself repeatedly when walking. He interprets an unusually long wait — for a colleague to return a call, for his wife to arrive home on time — as evidence that something dangerous is unfolding. He has stopped going anywhere he has not been before, because he has come to believe that unfamiliar environments are ones in which he cannot know where the threat is or how close.

What finally brought Marcus to the intake appointment was a moment at work when he realized he had turned down a home visit for a vulnerable client — a client whose situation genuinely concerned him — because the address was in a neighborhood he did not know. He is most afraid, he said, that something fundamental about who he is has been permanently altered. What he is hoping for, more cautiously, is to be able to do his job again.
